identity.title: Coupling Experts and Routers in Mixture-of-Experts via an Auxiliary Loss

problem.claim: Aligning MoE router decisions with expert capabilities.

gap.claim: MoE models lack explicit constraints enforcing this alignment, which the authors say limits performance.

contributions.claim: Introduces expert-router coupling (ERC), a lightweight auxiliary loss using perturbed router embeddings as proxy tokens and two-way activation constraints.
Uses only n² activations, yielding a fixed cost independent of batch size, unlike token-scaling prior coupling methods as characterized by the authors.
Provides flexible control and quantitative tracking of expert specialization during training.

stated_novelty.claim: The authors distinguish ERC by tightly coupling router decisions with expert capabilities at fixed n² activation cost.

author_reported_evidence.claim: The authors report demonstrating ERC effectiveness through pre-training MoE language models from 3B to 15B parameters and analysis over trillions of tokens.
The authors report that ERC enables specialization control and quantitative tracking during training.

narrative_sequence.summary: MoE routing lacks explicit alignment constraints between router decisions and expert capabilities.
ERC represents each expert with a router-embedding proxy token and evaluates perturbed proxies through the experts.
The loss imposes reciprocal preference constraints: experts favor their own proxy, and proxies favor their corresponding expert.
The stated constraints target faithful router representations, expert specialization, and fixed n² computational cost.
The authors report large-scale pre-training and specialization analysis, including models from 3B to 15B parameters and trillions of tokens.

source_observation.claim: The abstract defines alignment through two reciprocal, testable activation inequalities rather than a single router-side objective.

lessons.interpretation: A concrete decomposition can make an alignment claim more operational and expose whether both sides of a relationship are covered.
lessons.application: When proposing an alignment objective, specify complementary directional constraints and identify the measurable signal each one compares.
lessons.exception: This framing may be unsuitable when the system has no meaningful paired entities or when one-directional alignment is the intended objective.

unknowns: The abstract reports effectiveness but gives no quantitative results, baselines, or evaluation metrics.
The computational comparison with prior coupling methods is stated qualitatively; implementation and constant-factor costs are unspecified.
The abstract does not establish independently verified correctness, reproducibility, or priority over prior work.
